q: How much of the reported anisotropy in Janicki et al.'s Figure 7 comes from the bound-sphere geometric constraint per se, versus from the 2D-indexed DFT ecoord table? An ablation is missing.
basis: Section 2.2 conflates two independent mechanisms (bound-sphere lattice-enforced pairing vs 2D-indexed rate table) but reports no ablation. Our 10-seed surrogate on the same HCP lattice with a monotonic 1D ecoord ladder is markedly more isotropic than the paper's experimental peaks, which suggests the 2D ecoord table is doing much of the work. But we cannot separate the two without the actual disphere code.
next_steps: (a) Ask the authors to publish the diffusion/disphere app + resv lattice code (which the paper says is on the resveratrol branch but is not there as of commit f6bcc3b, 2025-03-31). (b) Once released, run 3 versions: (i) 1D ecoord + single-sphere, (ii) 1D ecoord + bound-sphere, (iii) 2D ecoord + bound-sphere. Compare the resulting W:L and H:L peaks. (c) If the disphere code is genuinely embargoed, reimplement disphere as an external app-style patch and rerun the ablation with just the paper's 74-point DFT table.

q: Does the 'arbitrarily large barrier' imputation for un-tabulated coordinations bias the reported facet ordering toward the specific 74-point sampling geometry of the DFT library?
basis: Section 3.1 says untabulated coordinations receive an arbitrarily large barrier. That is effectively an infinite acceptance penalty and could lock in the specific facet ordering that DFT happened to sample. Section 3.2 reports strong single-direction anisotropy in trajectories, which is exactly the kind of qualitative outcome that a hard-barrier imputation could artificially amplify. No sensitivity study to (i) finite penalty (e.g. 3x max_tabulated) or (ii) nearest-tabulated interpolation is reported.
next_steps: Rerun the paper's protocol with three imputation policies for coordination patterns outside the 74-point DFT set: (a) hard block (as published), (b) finite penalty = 3x max tabulated, (c) nearest-tabulated-coordination interpolation. Report the shift in the H:L and W:L histogram peaks and the fraction of accepted depositions that end up on imputed sites. If (a) vs (c) differ by >20% in either peak, the imputation is a significant methodological knob that should be reported in future papers.

q: There is an apparent inconsistency between '48x16x24 unit cells' and '~200 nm x 250 nm x 210 nm' in Section 3.2 given literature P2_1/c resveratrol unit-cell parameters. Which is the correct box description?
basis: From the P2_1/c resveratrol unit cell (a=7.6 A, b=24.5 A, c=15.9 A per Chadha et al. 2016, cited by the paper as [45]), 48x16x24 unit cells is approximately 365 x 392 x 382 nm — 1.5-2x larger than the stated 200 x 250 x 210 nm. This makes it hard to verify volumetric quantities and to cross-check surface-vs-bulk ratios. Our replicate box (56 x 13.86 x 39.19 site units for HCP 1.0) confirms 48x16x24 primitive HCP cells but the mapping to actual resveratrol nanometers is under-specified in the paper.
next_steps: Contact the authors to get the actual lattice-parameter mapping used in `lattice resv 1.0`. Once the mapping is known, verify (a) whether the box description in Section 3.2 was in unit-cells or in real length, (b) whether the growth-rate estimates in the paper implicitly assume one or the other, and (c) publish a corrigendum if needed. In this replication we assumed the unit-cell reading was correct and reported HCP site-units.

q: Is 5x10^6 KMC trial steps per run x 560 replicates sufficient to converge the simulated aspect-ratio histogram, and does the reported 'much narrower simulated distribution than experiment' reflect under-sampling versus over-simplified physics?
basis: The paper reports simulated aspect-ratio distributions are much narrower than experiment but attributes this entirely to 'variation in initial nuclei shape upon cooling' in experiment. No convergence-vs-N_trial or convergence-vs-N_replicate curve is shown. Without such curves it is not possible to distinguish under-sampling from a genuine physical narrowness of the simulated ensemble.
next_steps: Run the paper's exact protocol at 3 trial-step counts (10^6, 5x10^6 as published, 2x10^7) and 3 replicate counts (100, 560 as published, 2000). Plot histogram peak position and full-width-half-max as a function of both. If the peak/FWHM has visibly not plateaued at 5x10^6 x 560, the narrowness attribution in Section 3.3 is at least partly a sampling artifact, and the paper's 'peaks overlap' comparison should be revisited with an converged run.

q: Can an isotropic 1D ecoord ladder inverse-fit to Micro-CT aspect ratios approximately recover the DFT-derived 2D rate table, and if so how much of the paper's parametric machinery is compressible?
basis: Our surrogate 1D isotropic ladder is much more isotropic than experiment (W:L=0.53 vs experimental ~0.35), so an inverse fit is well-posed in the right direction. If the DFT rate table has an approximately-low-rank structure when projected to 1D coordination, this would be a strong compression / validation cross-check on the DFT library. If not, that itself is a useful negative result showing the 2D indexing is genuinely necessary.
next_steps: Fit a 12-parameter 1D ecoord ladder to the reported experimental Micro-CT aspect-ratio distributions (H:L and W:L) using a KMC-in-the-loop optimizer (e.g. Bayesian optimization with the aspect-ratio JS-divergence to Micro-CT as the loss). Compare the fitted ladder against the diagonal projection of the paper's 2D DFT table. Report (a) whether the fit reaches the Micro-CT distribution, (b) the KL/JS distance between fitted-ladder and DFT-projected-ladder, and (c) the residual gap that only 2D indexing can close. This exercise is possible today with only the released code (the surrogate replicate here is a small step toward it).
